newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: U.S. "hopeful but sceptical" on Iran - Cohen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. "hopeful but sceptical" on Iran - Cohen.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen met Saudi Arabia's King Fahd on Saturday and told reporters Washington was "hopeful but sceptical" that Iran would give up its support of international terrorism following a recent election.

But he also said in an interview on his plane en route to Jeddah that the United States would not soften its hardline policy toward Iran unless there were signs it had changed its attitude toward the West and its opposition to the Middle East peace process.
The recent election of moderate cleric Mohammad Khatami as Iran's president has raised hopes that Tehran would soften its own tough policy toward the West.
"We remain hopeful but sceptical" on Iran, Cohen told reporters. "For the time being our policy is going to remain constant."
Cohen spent 30 minutes with King Fahd and the two confirmed the "firm and unshakeable" relationship between the two countries, U.S. Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters.

Bacon said that the king, who has had health problems in recent years, was "lively and responsive" during the meeting at his palace and that Cohen had emphasised continued U.S. support for Saudi security.
"He (the king) shook hands with everybody. He was engaged and they exchanged jokes," said Bacon, adding that the king had asked about U.S. President Bill Clinton's knee, injured in a recent fall.
Cohen's visit will also take him to Kuwait, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Oman before flying home Wednesday.

Referring to last month's election of Khatami, seen as more moderate than his predecessor Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Cohen told reporters in an interview: "We need to see some signs on the part of the Iranians that this (election) will mark a change in their behaviour.

"As long as they continue to support terrorism, as long as they continue to develop weapons of mass destruction, as long as they try to upset the Middle East peace process, then our policy toward them is not going to change."

Some moderate Gulf states, including Qatar and Oman, have suggested that Washington should open a dialogue with Iran as a step toward ending U.S. attempts to isolate Tehran financially and diplomatically. Iran denies that it supports terrorism.
"Obviously there are some people looking with hopefulness that this recent election represents a change," Cohen said.
"But we will have to wait and see. It will be some time before he (Khatami) settles into office and, I suspect, some time before physical changes would take place."

It was Cohen's first visit as Defence Secretary to the potentially volatile region where the United States sent more than 500,000 troops for the 1991 Gulf War, in which a U.S.-led military coalition drove occupying Iraqi forces from Kuwait.

Washington still maintains a major naval fleet in the Gulf based in Bahrain and has nearly 200 attack jets in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, keeping watch over southern Iraq. Cohen will visit some of the more than 4,000 U.S. airmen at Prince Sultan airbase in the Saudi desert on Sunday.

U.S. relations with the Saudis have at times been strained in the past year over Saudi handling of the investigation of a car bomb at the Khobar Towers military housing complex in Dhahran last June 25 that killed 19 U.S. airmen.

"So far, the evidence is still inconclusive and the investigation continues. We are not going to make any pre-judgment on that," Cohen said aboard his plane when asked if there was any evidence that Iran had supported the Khobar Towers attack.
